> **Proposed API.** This guide follows `docs/api-vision.md`. The implementation
> has not been changed to match it. All code is non-executable; no credentials
> were read, callbacks invoked, or provider operations performed.

Choosing a client should not secretly sign you in. Inspecting a route should
not test it by making a paid request. Building an already resolved request
should not call a credential function again.

The proposed API separates those actions so their names can be trusted.

```r
library(lm15)
```

## A client constructor creates a recipe

```r
client <- new_lm(
  "openai",
  credential = credential_env("OPENAI_API_KEY")
)
```

`credential_env()` describes where an API key will come from. Neither it nor
`new_lm()` reads the variable. The client can exist before the source is
available. Supplied option names, value types and endpoint combinations are
checked before any identity source is acquired.

For a provider's standard resolution chain, use the default recipe:

```r
client <- new_lm("xai", credential = credential_auto())
```

This retains lm15's declared subscription-before-billing rules. It is not a
new R-specific chain. If a selected renewable subscription fails, a later paid
key is not silently substituted.

The preferred argument is `credential`, because it can represent more than an
API key:

```r
client <- new_lm(
  "azure",
  credential = credential_env("APP_ACCESS_TOKEN", kind = "bearer_token"),
  settings = host_settings(resource = "my-resource")
)
```

The old `api_key` spelling remains a compatibility alias. Supplying both names
is an error, not a choice decided by map order or comparing secret values.
There is no inference of credential kind from the characters in a token.

## Let one settings value describe the host

```r
client <- new_lm(
  "bedrock-chat",
  credential = credential_auto(),
  settings = host_settings(region = "eu-west-1")
)
```

`host_settings()` checks the shared vocabulary of named host fields. A provider
then checks which of those fields it supports. Settings are not smuggled into
a model string, and missing required data is not replaced by a guessed region.
Declared provider defaults stay visible in the resolution report.

`compat` and `base_url` remain separate choices. A compatibility preset selects
a server's declared format details and, where declared, its default address:

```r
local_client <- new_lm(
  "openai-chat",
  credential = api_key("local"),
  compat = "lmstudio"
)
```

This is still a recipe. It does not connect to the local server. A preset with
no declared address cannot silently fall back to a paid cloud endpoint.

## Inspect the same recipe you will use

```r
report <- explain_auth(client)
report
```

Inspection may read local source presence and credential-file metadata. It
does not call a custom credential function, run a CLI, renew credentials or
contact a provider. Deferred work is reported as deferred/unprobed, not as a
successful authentication check.

“Configured”, “credential available”, “permitted to use this model”, and
“request succeeded” remain different claims. Automatic printing reveals
source kinds and safe structural information, not values or signed material.

For deterministic application configuration, `env = character()` means no
ambient environment variables. A supplied named vector is an explicit input;
`env = NULL` means consult the process environment later when resolving a source.

## Route model names without opening a connection

```r
router <- new_router(
  credentials = list(openai = credential_env("OPENAI_API_KEY"))
)

resolve(router, "openai:gpt-4.1-mini")
resolve(router, "gpt-4.1-mini")
explain_auth(router, model = "openai:gpt-4.1-mini")
```

Resolution uses an explicit prefix, supplied catalog, or declared rule. It
never tries several providers until one works. The `credentials` map retains
the shared-key rule and exact-entry precedence. Its old `api_keys` spelling
is an exclusive compatibility alias, not a second source of truth.

`router_lm(router, model)` returns a reusable client recipe. A configuration or
identity change cannot reuse another identity's token. Reusing a client is not
caching model responses or caching the result of a user credential function.

## Keep metadata value-like and advisory

```r
catalog <- new_model_registry(list(
  model_info("acme-model", "openai", "openai_responses", aliases = list("short-name"))
))

larger_catalog <- registry_add(
  catalog,
  model_info("second-model", "gemini", "gemini_generate_content")
)

router <- new_router(catalog = larger_catalog)
registry_get(catalog, "openai", "short-name")
resolve(router, "short-name")
```

`registry_add()` returns a new registry; it does not mutate `catalog` or an
existing router. Replacing an entry removes its old aliases. A router captures
the catalog value supplied to it, so a metadata change is deliberate.

Discovery is a separate operation:

```r
catalog <- discover_model_registry()
```

It can read packaged JSON catalogs or invoke explicitly supplied loader
functions. It processes a whole catalog before adding it and keeps the first
duplicate provider/model entry. Metadata helps identify a model; it never
changes the provider's request encoding rules.

## Resolve effects once, then encode without effects

Most applications should call `complete()` or `stream()`. For inspection and
transport integration, the HTTP preparation boundary is explicit:

```r
credential_reads <- 0L
credential <- function() {
  credential_reads <<- credential_reads + 1L
  bearer_token("example-only-token")
}

client <- new_lm("openai", credential = credential, env = character())
req <- request("gpt-4.1-mini", message_user("hello"))

prepared <- prepare_request(client, req)
wire <- build_request(prepared)
```

This illustrative credential function is part of the example, not an actual
login. The design promises no call during construction, one call during
preparation, and no further call during encoding.

Preparation may read media, acquire credentials, renew a stored login and
write a replacement under its lock. It checks all locally knowable request
and configuration errors first. It does not send the model inference request.
The prepared result binds the resolved identity, sources, signing time and
HTTP mode. It is short-lived, secret-bearing and not a cache or archive format.

`build_request(prepared)` performs no I/O. The existing two-argument
`build_request(client, req)` is retained as an effectful compatibility facade,
not relabelled pure. Realtime setup remains its own advanced connection/frame
surface rather than pretending to be one HTTP request.

If you inspect a preparation and then call `complete(client, req)`, completion
prepares a fresh operation. It does not send the earlier inspected object.
Printing either prepared or wire objects must hide addresses, headers and
bodies that may contain credentials.

## Fail before doing unintended work

A proposed diagnostic for a misspelled argument is:

```r
new_lm("openai", credentail = obtain_credential())
```

```text
Error in new_lm():
  Unused argument: `credentail`.
  Did you mean `credential`?
  The unused argument was not evaluated.
```

That is an illustrative design expectation, not captured output.
`obtain_credential()` is deliberately an unevaluated example expression: the
rejection must not run it or print its contents. Input errors should identify
safe argument names and R field paths, while provider errors keep the shared
LM15 classes and codes.

A valid canonical setting can still be unsupported by a provider. That remains
a refusal, not a field the client silently removes. Credentials, endpoint
selection and model behavior must never become global convenience options.

## Preserve the migration door's meaning

```r
resolve(router, "gpt-4.1-mini")
resolve_openai_chat(router, "gpt-4.1-mini")
openai_chat_model_string("groq/openai/gpt-oss-20b")
```

A bare OpenAI model imported from Chat Completions keeps that endpoint. An
explicit `openai:model` prefix still means Responses. Native lm15 code builds
canonical requests; `complete_from_openai_chat(router, body)` is the deliberate
foreign-format boundary. It does not accept client keys, retry policy or
timeouts hidden inside the request body.
